item.title: StraitsX, OCBC, Standard Chartered explore interoperability between tokenized deposits networks
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered have completed a proof of concept (POC) exploring how tokenized deposits issued by different banks can be used for payments between financial institutions.
item.content:encoded:
StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered have completed a proof of concept (POC) exploring how tokenized deposits issued by different banks can be used for payments between financial institutions.

The parties developed and tested the model through a POC under the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) BLOOM initiative, addressing a growing interoperability challenge as banks develop their own tokenized deposit ecosystems, the trio said in a statement on Thursday.

As tokenized deposits represent claims against their issuing banks only, they cannot be seamlessly transferred across different banks’ tokenized deposit ecosystems, which may operate on different platforms and standards.

The POC demonstrated how StraitsX’s shared settlement infrastructure could coordinate payments to achieve end-to-end settlement across OCBC’s and Standard Chartered’s tokenized deposit ecosystems, including payment initiation, compliance screening, liquidity checks, settlement and confirmation.

The participants also observed that the shared model reduced the need for bilateral prefunding arrangements, demonstrating the potential for more efficient liquidity management compared with conventional models. The POC follows frameworks established under BLOOM.

It is noted that many traditional interbank USD payment flows operate within fixed settlement windows and are unavailable outside business hours.

Tokenized deposits on distributed ledgers can settle in near real-time and outside conventional banking hours. To realize that potential across institutions, however, different banks’ tokenized deposit ecosystems need to be able to work together.

Through the controlled POC, StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered tested payment flows using tokenized deposits from both participating banks.

StraitsX coordinated payment instructions and transaction information between the institutions, supported screening coordination and settlement after applicable compliance, eligibility and liquidity checks.

The POC successfully completed USD payment flows outside conventional banking cut-off windows, demonstrating how interoperable tokenized deposit infrastructure could enable always-on value movement across participating banks’ separate tokenized deposit ecosystems within minutes, including the necessary compliance, liquidity and settlement processes.

It showed how tokenized deposits from different issuers could be treated as equivalent within a shared interoperability framework, providing an early indication of how a shared interoperability model could support faster, always-on institutional payments while reducing the need for bilateral prefunding arrangements.

As more financial institutions explore tokenized forms of money, further development will require assessment of the legal, regulatory, operational and commercial arrangements needed for broader implementation, including settlement finality, liquidity management, participant responsibilities and financial-crime controls.

“Tokenized deposits have the potential to enable near-instant and programmable money movement, but their broader utility will depend on how effectively different banking ecosystems can connect,” said Tianwei Liu, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of StraitsX.

“Together with OCBC and Standard Chartered, we are exploring how shared settlement infrastructure can support that interoperability while reducing the need for bilateral arrangements and prefunded liquidity between individual participants,” he added.

Meanwhile, Carmen Chan, Deputy Head, Global Transaction Banking, OCBC. said tokenized deposits can bring the trust of commercial bank money into an increasingly digital and always-on economy.

“Their full potential, however, will depend on interoperability across banking ecosystems,

“Through MAS’ BLOOM initiative, we are exploring with industry partners how shared infrastructure could enable seamless value movement across banks, while preserving the regulatory safeguards, integrity of bank deposits and trusted banking relationships that underpin the financial system,” she said.

She also said this collaboration is an important step towards understanding how interoperable tokenized deposits could support the future of institutional payments.

Ankur Kanwar, Head of Transaction Banking & Cash Management, Singapore & ASEAN, Global Head of Payment and Treasury Solutions, Standard Chartered, said for digital assets to scale, the industry needs to move beyond individual solutions towards a more connected and interoperable financial ecosystem.

“That requires collaboration across institutions to build the trust, credibility and connectivity needed for broader adoption. Standard Chartered’s approach is centered on helping orchestrate that ecosystem, connecting capabilities and participants so that tokenized assets and different forms of money can work together more effectively,

“Collaborations like this are an important part of turning that ambition into practical, scalable infrastructure,” he added.

NETS, Ant International deepen partnership to expand Singapore’s digital payments ecosystem

item.title: Yeahka and Mastercard demonstrate agent-pay purchase in Singapore
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Yeahka and Mastercard demonstrated an AI-assisted bubble-tea purchase that moved from product discovery to authorized payment in one conversation.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong-listed payment technology company Yeahka and Mastercard have demonstrated an artificial intelligence-assisted purchase that moved from product discovery to payment within a single conversation at the Singapore FinTech Festival.

The demonstration used a bubble-tea order to show how an AI agent could search nearby merchants, retrieve product information, build an order and initiate payment after the consumer confirmed the transaction. The companies also signed a cooperation agreement to explore further agent-driven commerce applications.

Under the setup described in Yeahka’s November 19 announcement, Mastercard’s app served as the consumer interface. It integrated an AI-agent payment service from YeahPay, Yeahka’s international payments brand, while Yeahka subsidiary Fushi Tech supplied merchant and product information.

A consumer could ask the agent to find a nearby bubble-tea shop and order a drink. The system then used Fushi Tech’s merchant services to identify stores and display products, prices, sizes and toppings. After the consumer selected an item and confirmed the order, the agent initiated the transaction through YeahPay. The payment remained subject to user authorization and security checks.

The example was a festival demonstration rather than evidence of a broad commercial rollout. Yeahka said the companies intend to explore integrations that connect product discovery, order creation and payment, but it did not disclose a launch timetable, merchant coverage or transaction volume for the arrangement.

The Singapore demonstration gives the collaboration a direct Asia-Pacific use case as payment networks and regional fintech companies test how software agents can act on verified consumer instructions. Mastercard and Ant International separately announced a live consumer transaction and a machine-payment pilot in Singapore this week, while Visa has expanded an Asia-Pacific program intended to prepare acquirers, payment providers and merchants for agent-initiated transactions.

Agent-led payments require controls that conventional online checkout flows do not always expose directly. A provider must verify the software agent, confirm that the user authorized it to act and ensure that an instruction remains within the user’s permissions. YeahPay said it is exploring payment protocols, identity verification and delegated-authorization mechanisms for those requirements.

Yeahka said developers can access YeahPay’s AI-agent payment software development kit and technical documentation from its website. The company is listed in Hong Kong under stock code 9923 and operates payment and merchant technology businesses through YeahPay and Fushi Tech.

YeahPay targets the trust gap holding back autonomous AI shopping

item.title: YeePay and Finmo connect cross-border payments into China
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: YeePay and Finmo agreed on a direct integration for eligible businesses to make renminbi payments to recipients in mainland China.
item.content:encoded:
China-based payment provider YeePay and Singapore-headquartered treasury platform Finmo have agreed on a direct integration that will let eligible Finmo clients make renminbi payments to businesses and other recipients in mainland China.

The companies announced the partnership at the Singapore FinTech Festival on November 19. They said the service is intended for international businesses that need to pay suppliers, employees and contractors in China while managing the transactions through Finmo’s existing platform.

Under the arrangement described in YeePay’s announcement, Finmo will connect to YeePay’s local payment infrastructure, transaction-verification tools and payment-tracing capabilities. YeePay will gain access to Finmo’s international licensing network and overseas merchant relationships.

The companies said eligible payments will be processed in Chinese yuan, subject to applicable regulations and the commercial arrangements between the partners. They did not disclose a general-availability date, pricing, transaction limits or expected payment volume.

The integration has a concrete Asia-Pacific focus. Finmo was founded in Singapore and holds a Major Payment Institution license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, along with licenses or registrations in markets including Australia, Hong Kong, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States and Dubai. YeePay operates a cross-border payment network centered on access to China and other international markets.

Finmo launched a multi-currency business account earlier in November that allows companies to collect, hold, convert and pay across currencies. The company said the account can collect more than 45 currencies, hold more than 27 and send payments to more than 195 countries and territories through its licenses and partner network.

The new YeePay connection adds a route for payments into mainland China from the same treasury environment. Finmo said clients will be able to initiate yuan payments without moving to a separate system, providing a consolidated view of payment status and transaction records.

Finmo raised $18.5 million in a Series A round in February 2025 led by Quona Capital and PayPal Ventures, with Citi Ventures participating. YeePay said its network supports payments and real-time foreign-exchange conversion across more than 100 currencies and serves businesses in travel, aviation, retail, cross-border e-commerce and international trade.

The partners said the integration will be governed by applicable regulatory requirements, but the announcement did not identify the specific client markets that will receive access first.

Finmo launches Business Account for cross-border SMEs, adding licensed multi-currency money movement to Finmo Treasury

item.title: Workday expands native payroll across four Asia-Pacific markets
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Workday is expanding native payroll to Singapore, Malaysia, New Zealand and Hong Kong, with staged availability running through 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Workday is expanding its native payroll software to four Asia-Pacific markets as part of a seven-market rollout that will extend the company’s payroll coverage across the region, Europe and Latin America.

The enterprise software company said in a November 18 announcement that it is adding Hong Kong, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore to its native payroll footprint. Mexico, the Netherlands and Spain make up the rest of the expansion.

Singapore is the first Asia-Pacific market in the rollout. Workday said early-adopter access is available there now, with general availability planned for January 2027. Early access in New Zealand is scheduled for December 2026, followed by general availability in April 2027.

Malaysia is due to enter early access in February 2027 and reach general availability in June. Workday plans to release its Hong Kong payroll offering sequentially from 2027 alongside the new products for Mexico, the Netherlands and Spain.

AI supports local payroll development

Workday said it is using artificial intelligence to accelerate parts of the development process for each market, including research into local requirements, payroll calculations, testing and documentation. The company said payroll experts, engineers and local specialists review and validate the AI-generated work, while automated tests are used to check results.

Using that approach, Workday said it launched the Singapore early-adopter program 10 times faster than its previous country rollouts. The comparison is a company-supplied measure and Workday did not disclose the baseline development time in its announcement.

The company is also preparing autopilot capabilities for its Payroll Agent, which works with an organization’s payroll data, policies and settings. Workday said the agent will run checks before and after payroll processing, flag potential errors and prepare suggested corrections for payroll teams to approve. Early-adopter access to those capabilities is planned for early 2027.

Regional payroll systems draw investment

The rollout adds another multinational provider to a regional payroll technology market that includes companies building localized services and cross-border platforms. In July, TNGlobal reported that India-based AscentHR acquired Malaysia’s OS HRS to expand its payroll delivery and compliance capabilities across Asia-Pacific.

Workday’s expansion also follows its broader push to apply AI across human resources, finance and information technology workflows. In a recent TNGlobal interview, the company discussed how fragmented enterprise systems can limit productivity gains from AI tools.

Workday said its native payroll products are intended to let multinational customers manage more country operations within one system, while its partner-based services cover additional markets. The new market releases and Payroll Agent features remain subject to change before their planned availability dates.

Workday’s Jess O’Reilly on why AI productivity gains get lost between disconnected systems [Q&A]

item.title: KLA opens second phase of Singapore semiconductor facility
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: KLA has opened Building 22B in Singapore, adding 210,000 square feet for semiconductor equipment production and outlining another possible expansion.
item.content:encoded:
KLA Corporation has opened the second phase of a major expansion at its Ang Mo Kio manufacturing site in Singapore, adding about 210,000 square feet of operations space for advanced semiconductor equipment production.

The new Building 22B is fully operational, the US-based process-control equipment maker said in a November 20 announcement. Together with Building 22A, which opened in October 2024, the Building 22 complex now covers about 420,000 square feet.

The facility includes Class 100, or ISO 5, cleanrooms, engineering and laboratory areas, offices and warehouse space. KLA said the additional capacity will support equipment used in advanced packaging, silicon photonics and artificial intelligence-related semiconductor applications.

Singapore is a major node in the global semiconductor supply chain. The sector contributes about 6 percent of the country’s gross domestic product and employs more than 35,000 people, according to the Singapore Economic Development Board.

KLA also outlined a possible further expansion in Singapore, subject to final land arrangements and regulatory approvals. The company said Building 22B and the proposed next phase are expected over the longer term to support about 1,000 additional positions across research and development, supply chain and manufacturing engineering.

That jobs estimate includes positions tied to a future phase that has not yet received final approval. KLA did not disclose the investment value or construction timetable for the proposed additional expansion.

KLA established a Singapore sales and service operation in 1996 and began manufacturing in the country in 2006. Its Singapore activities now include research and development, manufacturing, corporate functions and one of the company’s largest technical training centers.

Cindy Koh, executive vice president at the Singapore Economic Development Board, said the facility would deepen the country’s semiconductor-equipment capabilities and create roles in manufacturing engineering and research and development, alongside training and upskilling opportunities.

The latest opening completes the second phase described when KLA unveiled Building 22A in 2024. TNGlobal reported at the time that the first phase formed part of a $200 million expansion and that the second structure was scheduled to bring the site’s total capacity to about 420,000 square feet.

KLA said it will continue working with Singapore universities and polytechnics on internships and industry input into curricula. The November 20 opening ceremony was attended by Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins and KLA Singapore country president Theo Kneepkens.

US’s KLA completes first phase of $200M Singapore operations expansion

item.title: NETS, Ant International deepen partnership to expand Singapore’s digital payments ecosystem
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Singapore’s payment services group Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) and Ant International are deepening their partnership to help businesses expand their customer reach and streamline operations as the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven commerce grows.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s payment services group Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) and Ant International are deepening their partnership to help businesses expand their customer reach and streamline operations as the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven commerce grows.

The duo signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) at the Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 to explore a collaboration that draws on NETS’ digital payments services and Ant International’s Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP) as well as its full stack of AI-native solutions, according to their statement on Thursday.

The expanded partnership spans several areas of strategic cooperation, included bringing agentic commerce capabilities to businesses of all sizes across Singapore.

NETS will become the first national payment rail to join Ant International’s AMP, an agentic payment protocol designed for mobile interfaces. As consumers hand more of their everyday decisions to AI agents – from discovery to checkout – merchants who can accept agent-initiated payments stay discoverable and transactable in the new world of agentic commerce.

The collaboration between Ant International and NETS will explore the opportunity for NETS App wallet users to grant trusted authorization for AI agents to initiate and complete payments, powered by AMP and for NETS to deploy AMP within its merchant acquiring infrastructure.

This allows NETS merchants – from heartland stalls to large enterprises to accept AI-initiated payments and bring agentic commerce into everyday payments across Singapore.

“For agentic commerce to scale, trust and accountability must be embedded by design. Working with Ant International, we will explore Know-Your-Agent (KYA) frameworks to help ensure AI agent transactions are secure and reliable, so that merchants can focus on growing their business,” said Lawrence Chan, Group Chief Executive Officer, NETS.

Peng Yang, Chief Executive Officer, Ant International, said agentic commerce is the next frontier, and no merchant should be left behind.

“Our full-stack AI-native solutions are designed to democratize AI, helping merchants of all sizes around the world grow,

“By working with our long-time strategic partner NETS, we aim to help businesses of every size across Singapore leverage AI to serve their customers everywhere, whether in-store, across borders or through AI agents,” he added.

Additionally, Ant International and NETS will explore interoperability between Know-Your-Agent (KYA) frameworks to enable more efficient onboarding and strengthen trust, accountability and risk visibility across both ecosystems.

Launched in April 2026, AMP is an open payment protocol built by Ant International for digital wallets, super apps, smart devices and other mobile interfaces to enable AI agents to execute payments.

In September, Ant International announced that 10 leading Alipay+ wallets and seven global acquiring partners were working with AMP on their own agentic commerce plans.

Alipay+ is Ant International’s global wallet ecosystem that connects more than two billion user accounts across over 50 international payment partners with more than 150 million merchants in 210+ markets, and 10+ national payment schemes, including Singapore’s SGQR.

Beyond agentic commerce, the partnership will help more businesses reach more customers. Alipay+ acceptance will extend beyond retail into new sectors such as SME F&B, allowing more local merchants to accept international e-wallets.

NETS and Ant International will explore to jointly develop an integrated merchant solution that combines NETS’ digital payment services with Ant International’s EPOS360, an AI-as-a-Service SME growth solution.

It will give merchants an integrated ecosystem to accept payments and manage daily operations, with AI capabilities to help them grow.

NETS will also explore embedded digital lending with ANEXT Bank Pte. Ltd., an affiliate of Ant International and a licensed digital wholesale bank in Singapore, to enable a seamless, fully digital end-to-end lending journey for NETS’ merchant ecosystem.

ST Engineering, OCBC test quantum-safe cybersecurity for financial services

item.title: AI company Everful raises $48.5M Series A, led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India, January Capital
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Everful, a builder of AI and data infrastructure for global commerce, has raised $48.5 million in a Series A financing led by two Singapore-based investors, namely Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital.
item.content:encoded:
Everful, a builder of AI and data infrastructure for global commerce, has raised $48.5 million in a Series A financing led by two Singapore-based investors, namely Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital.

In a statement on Friday, Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India said existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed also participated.

Everful was founded by Sisi Song, a former Alibaba Group executive and Bessemer Venture Partners investor, and Kevin Han, an AI entrepreneur. Everful currently ships more than 5 million pieces a month to retailers and brands in over 60 countries and partners with a fast-growing network of more than 30,000 vetted factories.

It has built an ever-expanding catalog of more than 20 million items and is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by year-end.

The new funding will deepen Everful’s presence in the U.S., its largest market, and in Europe, and expand its world model of commerce, AI agents, and fulfillment infrastructure.

Global commerce has a data problem, and much of the work still runs by hand. Most retailers and brands buy through layers of middlemen and endless email threads, with high minimum orders that eat into margins and leave them holding out-of-trend stock. The information needed to do better is scattered across thousands of sources in multiple languages, and no human team can keep up.

Two shifts change that. First, large language models and computer vision can read, reason over and act on messy, multilingual supply data at a scale that wasn’t possible even two years ago. Second, factories have digitized rapidly, holding ready stock and producing in small batches, so AI agents can now find and coordinate them in real time.

At Everful’s core is a world model of supply and demand. It maps what customers want, what factories can make and how to get products from one to the other. Everful’s AI agents use it to identify trending products, find and vet new factories, and manage all communications throughout each order. Every factory is continuously scored using quality data from Everful’s own inspections. Customers can buy wholesale, dropship or customize, all with low minimums, while Everful handles fulfillment end to end.

“Sourcing used to be a people problem. If you were big enough, you hired a team overseas to do it,” said Sisi Song, co-founder and CEO of Everful. “AI lets us turn that team into software. Now any business can operate as if it had a global sourcing team behind it, and this funding lets us bring that to many more businesses around the world.”

“We don’t build tools that leave the work to the customer. We build agents that deliver the result,” said Kevin Han, co-founder of Everful. “Every order, inspection and delivery feeds our world model of commerce, so the system gets smarter with each transaction. That’s what lets us operate at a speed and scale that traditional sourcing can’t match.”

“Small retailers struggle to find suppliers, and struggle even more to find ones they can trust,” said Jessica Koh, Senior Executive Director at Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India. “Everful is that partner, and it delivers at factory prices.”

“We’ve backed Sisi and Kevin since their first round,” said Alex Rankin, Partner at January Capital. “Their world model of commerce gets sharper with every order. That compounding data advantage is what AI infrastructure looks like.”

Thailand’s Horizon Group raises $12.5M from Singapore’s Vertex Ventures SE Asia & India

item.title: ST Engineering, OCBC test quantum-safe cybersecurity for financial services
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Singapore-based technology firm ST Engineering is working with lender OCBC to assess the bank's preparedness for quantum computing-related cybersecurity risks through a pilot under the Q-FINEX quantum-enabled financial infrastructure testbed, an initiative by the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN).
item.content:encoded:
Singapore-based technology firm ST Engineering is working with lender OCBC to assess the bank’s preparedness for quantum computing-related cybersecurity risks through a pilot under the Q-FINEX quantum-enabled financial infrastructure testbed, an initiative by the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN).

The pilot will use ST Engineering’s post-quantum cryptography readiness platform, Quantizant, to assess OCBC’s existing cybersecurity exposure and develop a prioritized roadmap for transitioning to quantum-safe cryptographic algorithms, ST Engineering said in a statement on Wednesday.

The assessment is aimed at helping the bank identify potential vulnerabilities in its current cryptographic systems and plan the transition to encryption methods designed to withstand attacks from future quantum computers.

Led by ST Engineering’s Enterprise (Digital) business, the initiative combines the group’s research in quantum computing and post-quantum cybersecurity to examine the implications of emerging quantum technologies for financial institutions.

Quantizant is designed to help organizations assess their exposure to quantum-related cybersecurity risks, plan a multi-year transition to quantum-safe cryptography and monitor compliance with relevant requirements.

The platform can also integrate with existing cybersecurity systems, allowing organizations to incorporate quantum readiness into their existing security management processes.

The pilot with OCBC is part of ST Engineering’s broader quantum research efforts under its Research Translation @ ST Engineering program, which was established in 2021.

Quantum computing was among the program’s initial research areas, with the group exploring potential applications in logistics optimization and cybersecurity.

ST Engineering is also expanding its research into quantum sensing, drawing on its capabilities in microelectronics, photonics, software and engineering to explore applications in border security, materials identification and industrial monitoring.

“Businesses will need to manage emerging risks, identify opportunities and create value in new ways as quantum technologies mature,” said Tan Bin Ru, president of Enterprise (Digital) at ST Engineering.

She said the collaboration with OCBC and GFTN would allow the group to apply its quantum capabilities to financial-sector challenges and advance the industry’s preparedness for the technology.

Singapore’s DBS partners Circle expand institutional access to USDC in Asia

item.title: India’s Paytm to invest up to $21M in Funding Societies payment subsidiary
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: India's Paytm will invest up to INR 2 billion ($21.4 million) in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Asia Group Pte Ltd (Funding Societies), including an initial investment of about INR 1.62 billion for a 19.1 percent stake in payment subsidiary CardUp Pte Ltd.
item.content:encoded:
India’s Paytm will invest up to INR 2 billion ($21.4 million) in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Asia Group Pte Ltd (Funding Societies), including an initial investment of about INR 1.62 billion for a 19.1 percent stake in payment subsidiary CardUp Pte Ltd.

In a filing to the Indian stock exchanges on Thursday, One 97 Communications Ltd, which operates Paytm, said its wholly owned subsidiary, Paytm Singapore Pte Ltd, had approved the proposed partnership with Funding Societies.

The initial investment in CardUp will amount to approximately INR 1.62 billion, while the remaining investment of about INR 380 million may be made in one of Funding Societies’ affiliates.

Under the partnership, Paytm will also establish a business and technology collaboration with CardUp, providing payments and lending technology to support the expansion of its technology-led payments and financial services offerings in Singapore.

Paytm said the arrangement is aligned with its previously announced strategy to expand into selected international markets through a “partner-operated” model.

Under this model, Paytm and its subsidiaries provide their payments acceptance platforms and technology-enabled devices, while local partners oversee sales, distribution and on-the-ground merchant operations.

The company will generate revenue through licensing fees, revenue-sharing and other arrangements, while keeping its capital deployment relatively limited.

Separately, Paytm said it had completed an additional investment of INR 5 billion in its wholly owned subsidiary, Paytm Cloud Technologies Ltd (PCTL).

Following the investment, PCTL has also completed an additional investment of INR 5 billion in Paytm Singapore, which is a step-down wholly owned subsidiary of One 97 Communications.

The proposed investments are subject to confirmatory due diligence, customary corporate approvals, execution of definitive agreements and relevant regulatory approvals.

Funding Societies secures new financing facility from Malaysia Debt Ventures Berhad

item.title: MAS flags financial stability risks as AI agents gain access to financial services
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents to manage payments, allocate funds and make financial decisions could pose risks to financial stability, prompting regulators and financial institutions to strengthen safeguards over how these autonomous systems access and transact through financial services.
item.content:encoded:
The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents to manage payments, allocate funds and make financial decisions could pose risks to financial stability, prompting regulators and financial institutions to strengthen safeguards over how these autonomous systems access and transact through financial services.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said consumers and businesses must retain meaningful control over the objectives, mandates and actions of their AI agents, warning that greater autonomy must be accompanied by clear accountability and appropriate controls.

MAS managing director Chia Der Jiun said the adoption of AI agents could accelerate the movement of money and allocation of assets, potentially prompting financial institutions to impose limits on agent-directed transactions to manage risks.

“As agents move into activities with financial consequences, authority, accountability and control become essential,” he said in his keynote address at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 on Thursday.

Chia highlighted several challenges arising from the use of personal AI agents in financial transactions, including whether financial institutions can establish that an agent has been authorized by a customer and whether it is acting within the scope of its mandate.

There are also questions over who should bear responsibility when an AI agent executes an incorrect transaction or acts beyond the instructions given to it.

He cautioned consumers against providing personal AI agents with their financial account login credentials, saying there was insufficient assurance that such access could be provided safely.

To address these concerns, MAS is working with the financial industry to develop a trusted protocol and secure channel through which AI agents can access financial services.

The initiative forms part of its Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) program, which seeks to establish safeguards for interactions between AI agents and financial institutions.

Chia said lessons from the first phase of SAFR highlighted four principles for safe agentic finance: bounded autonomy, clear identification and authority, specific mandates, and proportionate controls.

AI agents should be given sufficient discretion to perform useful tasks but remain within clearly defined boundaries. Their identities and authority must also be established, while mandates should specify permissible actions, limits and conditions.

In the next phase of SAFR, MAS will facilitate the development of a “know your agent” protocol to enable trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions.

The protocol will cover an agent’s identity and whom it represents, the authority granted to it, the mandate under which it operates, and the assurance surrounding its origin and reliability.

This would allow financial institutions to determine the terms and scope under which an agent could access their services, as well as establish secure channels for agent transactions.

MAS will also establish an Agentic Money Sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute to explore the integration of AI agents and programmable money in corporate treasury management and payment services.

For corporate treasury management, AI agents could monitor liquidity positions and upcoming payments, determine when and where funds should be transferred, and execute permitted transactions using tokenized deposits.

For payment services, banks and payment service providers could allow customer agents to execute payment instructions using digital money, including tokenized deposits and stablecoins. Participating institutions would verify agents’ identities and authority before applying appropriate risk controls.

Beyond financial transactions, MAS is also examining how the wider adoption of AI agents could reshape financial institutions, business models, markets and the broader economy.

Chia said AI agents could significantly reduce the costs and time involved in searching, comparing, negotiating and executing transactions, potentially resulting in more frequent and faster consumer and business decisions.

Consumers could use AI agents to compare products, prices and terms across multiple providers, negotiate on their behalf and monitor price movements to secure better deals.

Businesses could also automate procurement and inventory management, while accessing a wider pool of suppliers and continuously comparing prices, delivery times and contractual terms.

However, the increased speed and frequency of transactions could introduce new risks to market competition and pricing behaviour.

Chia noted that emerging studies of agent interactions in simulated environments had identified the possibility of agent collusion, even without explicit instructions to collude. Such behaviour could result in higher prices or weaker competition.

There were also concerns that more capable AI agents could secure better prices and terms than less capable ones, potentially creating unequal access to economic opportunities depending on the quality of AI models available.

He said agent-to-agent interactions could eventually give rise to dynamic markets in which prices and commercial terms are continuously determined through negotiations between autonomous systems.

Financial institutions may therefore need to strengthen their value propositions to both customers and AI agents, while considering whether transaction limits are necessary to manage risks arising from increasingly autonomous financial activities.

Chia said regulators would need to consider the implications of AI agents’ participation in financial markets and their ability to move money at greater speed.

MAS’ approach is to work with the financial industry to develop common standards, governance practices and infrastructure to support the safe adoption of the technology.

He said regulatory clarity, clearly defined governance responsibilities and industry collaboration would be important in enabling the financial sector to adopt transformative technologies while maintaining resilience.

Ultimately, MAS aims to develop an interoperable ecosystem that enables trusted interactions between AI agents, financial institutions and digital money, while ensuring that meaningful human control and accountability remain central to the development of the agentic economy.

Singapore’s A*STAR AI Institute, MAS-established Future of Finance Institute sign AI research deal
